1A — Aluminium

PDF pages 7–8
PDF page 7
1A Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                     Aluminium
Aluminium powder                                                                                            Al (26.98)
            Flammable solid [H228]. In contact with water releases flammable gases [H261].
            Aluminium powder is dangerous in contact with:
            • WATER. Under very hot conditions, hydrogen is formed. ACIDS and ALKALIS. Hydrogen is formed.
            • ALCOHOLS. Violent reactions occur after a lengthy induction period.
            • HALOGENS, ORGANOHALOGENS. SULFUR. Violent or explosive reactions occur.
            • METAL OXIDES, NITRATES(V), CHLORATES and other SOLID OXIDISING AGENTS. Explosive mixtures form.
  DANGER    • MERCURY and its COMPOUNDS (includes solutions). Rapid oxidation of aluminium occurs, may cause ignition.

            WEL (mg m-3): 10 (LTEL), 30 (STEL), as inhalable dust; 4 (LTEL), 12 (STEL), as respirable dust.
               Storage code: FW                                                                        [Dull-grey powder]
Storage        • An oxide layer forms on turnings and powder (which is particularly prone to oxidation). This surface
                 oxide reduces the activity of the metal. Keep containers tightly closed and dry.

Aluminium foil                                                                                           Al (26.98)
Currently not classified as hazardous.
Aluminium foil is dangerous in contact with:
• ACIDS and ALKALIS. Hydrogen is formed.
• HALOGENS. Violent reactions occur.
• MERCURY and its COMPOUNDS (includes solutions). Rapid oxidation of aluminium occurs which may cause ignition

Storage        Storage code: GIn                                                                             [Shiny-silver metal]

            Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies • If aluminium powder catches fire: Although difficult to ignite, the powder burns vigorously and is difficult
              to extinguish. If safe to do so, extinguish small fires by smothering with clean, dry sand (keep a container of
              sand specifically for this purpose).

foil                  on reverse.

                      Follow general guidance in About Hazcards (GL 120). NOTE for small amounts of aluminium powder:
                      • WSpec: Work in a fume cupboard. Ensure no naked flames. Add 10 g of the powder to 1 litre of 2 M
Disposal                hydrochloric acid (in a bucket or large beaker). Ensure solution remains acidic (use an indicator); add more
                        acid if necessary. Leave mixture in the fume cupboard for an hour or until reaction appears to be complete.
                        Pour resulting solution down a foul-water drain, diluting it further with a bucket of water.

1B — Gallium

PDF page 9
1B Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                            Gallium
Detailed information on the health hazards associated with gallium is limited/incomplete. Use gallium with great care.

Gallium                                                                                                                  Ga (69.72)
               Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314]. May be corrosive to metals [H290].
               Gallium is dangerous in contact with:
               • METALS (ESPECIALLY ALUMINIUM/ALUMINIUM ALLOYS). Gallium attacks metals by forming amalgams.
               • HALOGENS. Violent, exothermic reactions occur.
   DANGER
               • HYDROGEN PEROXIDE, HYDROCHLORIC ACID. Risk of explosions.

               Storage code: CS                                                                              [Silvery solid/liquid]
                                         o
               • Gallium melts at 29.8    C so may be a liquid on warm days.
               • It is sensitive to moist air and will tarnish if not kept dry.
               • Gallium should be supplied in a plastic container and it is best to keep it in this. Stand the container on a
                 layer of silica gel drying agent inside a secondary break-proof container. Keep the number of containers
Storage          used for gallium to a minimum. If a sample is split, use a plastic container similar to the original supplied.
               • Keep containers tightly closed.
               • Do NOT use metal containers.
               • Do NOT use glass containers.
                 - Once melted, gallium can be difficult to solidify as it exhibits ‘supercooling’ (remains liquid below its
                       melting/freezing point). However, when it does solidify, gallium expands and can crack glass.

               Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies
               • CORROSIVE (skin, eyes).

1B Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                                                       Gallium
Detailed information on the health hazards associated with gallium is limited/incomplete. Use gallium with great care.

Detailed guidance on specific activities and techniques involving these substances can be found at: www.cleapss.org.uk

General use of: Hazard information                         User Suggested general control measures and guidance
                                                                • Wear eye protection.
                                                                • Take particular care to avoid skin contact. If skin contact is likely, wear
                                                                  disposable nitrile gloves. In case of accidental contact, blackish stains
                                                                  may be visible; wash hands thoroughly with soap and water.
                                                                • Do not allow gallium to solidify in a glass container.


                                                                    Other notes; see also detailed activity-specific guidance:
Gallium                                                     TT      • Melting gallium (TT): Place the container inside a plastic bag (to
                                 DANGER
                                                                      protect the label). Stand this in a container of warm water.
                                                                    • Demonstrations using gallium (TT): See Supplementary Risk
                               CORROSIVE
                                                                      Assessment Investigating the properties of gallium metal (SRA 037)
                           (skin, eyes, metal)                        for detailed guidance; this includes Making a gallium spoon.



                                                                                                                                            Disposal: W3, W1

Disposal              Follow general guidance in About Hazcards (GL 120).

7 — Ammonium dichromate(VI), (NH4)2Cr2O7

PDF pages 33–34
PDF page 33
7 Risk Assessment Guidance                                      Ammonium dichromate(VI), (NH4)2Cr2O7
Ammonium dichromate(VI)                                                                                     (NH4)2Cr2O7 (252.07)
                   May intensify fire; oxidiser [H272]. Toxic if swallowed [H301]. Harmful in contact with skin [H312].
                   Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314]. May cause an allergic skin reaction [H317]. Fatal if
                   inhaled [H330]. May cause allergy or asthma symptoms or breathing difficulties if inhaled [H334]. May
                   cause genetic defects [H340]. May cause cancer [H350]. May damage fertility. May damage the unborn
                   child [H360FD]. Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure [H372]. Very toxic
                   to aquatic life with long lasting effects [H410].
                   Ammonium dichromate(VI) is dangerous in contact with:
                   • ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM, CARBON, SULFUR, PHOSPHORUS, COMBUSTIBLE MATERIALS, including
                     ORGANIC SUBSTANCES. The reactions are violent and may become explosive.

                     Never mix ammonium dichromate with metals, especially if powdered (eg, aluminium, magnesium).
    DANGER           Never heat ammonium dichromate in a confined space; explosion risk. See Other notes (reverse).

                   WEL (mg m-3): 0.01 (LTEL), 0.03 (STEL), Carc, Sen; as chromium (Cr)
                   Storage code: T                                                                           [Orange-red crystals]
Storage
                   • Do not store beside flammable liquids (FL) or other combustible materials (eg, organic chemicals (GOrg).


                   Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                   • CORROSIVE, OXIDISING, VERY TOXIC (skin, eyes, inhalation).

Emergencies        • General spills/clearing up: TOXIC, OXIDISING.
                     Collect up carefully to avoid raising dust. Be aware that heat, friction and fire (or other ignition
                     sources) can cause rapid ‘explosion-like’ decomposition. Small quantities of a spill may be treated as
                     described in Disposal (see reverse). Otherwise, retain for disposal by Registered Waste Carrier, W1.

Disposal                        Dissolve no more than 10 g of ammonium dichromate in about 250 cm3 of 1 M sulfuric acid. Add ~ 12 g of

8 — Ammonium salts: oxidising agents

PDF page 35
8 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                Ammonium salts: oxidising agents
   Ammonium salts must NOT be mixed or ground with potassium chlorate(V) or manganate(VII). Explosive mixtures may form.
Ammonium nitrate(V)                                                                                      NH4NO3 (80.04)
                   May intensify fire; oxidiser [H272]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. Suppliers may also indicate
                   one or more of the following: Causes skin irritation [H315]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
                   Ammonium nitrate(V) is dangerous in contact with:
                    ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM, SODIUM, POTASSIUM, CARBON, SULFUR, PHOSPHORUS. Explosive
                     mixtures are formed which are sensitive to movement.
                    POTASSIUM MANGANATE(VII). The mixture explodes spontaneously after a while.
                    ETHANOIC ACID and other ORGANIC COMPOUNDS. Unstable explosive mixtures are formed.
   WARNING            Do NOT grind this salt. Do NOT allow the salt to become contaminated with organic matter.
Storage                Storage code: Ox                                      [Colourless-white crystalline solid, hygroscopic]
Ammonium persulfate   (di)ammonium peroxodisulfate(VI)                                                  (NH4)2S2O8 (228.20)
                  May intensify fire; oxidiser [H272]. Harmful if swallowed [H302]. Causes skin irritation [H315]. May
                  cause an allergic skin reaction [H317]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. May cause allergy or asthma
                  symptoms or breathing difficulties if inhaled [H334]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
                  Ammonium peroxodisulfate(VI) is dangerous in contact with:
                   POWERED ALUMINIUM, ZINC. Explosive reactions may occur.
       DANGER  POTASSIUM CHLORATE(VII), POTASSIUM MANGANATE(VII). Explosive mixtures are formed.
                   HEAT. If heated strongly, it will explode.

                       Storage code: Ox                                                                [White crystalline solid]
Storage                Place bottle inside another lidded container with self-indicating silica gel. Pressure may build up in
                       bottles. Take care when opening.

Emergencies            Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

9C Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                     Ammonium salts: other (3)
Ammonium salts must NOT be mixed or ground with potassium chlorate(V) or manganate(VII), explosive mixtures may form.
Ammonium carbonate                           sal volatile (and ‘smelling salts’), salt of hartshorn                   (NH4)2CO3 (96.09)
Ammonium molybdate(VI)-4-water                                                                              (NH4)6Mo7O24.4H2O (1235.86)
                 Ammonium carbonate, molybdate*: Harmful if swallowed [H302].
                 Ammonium molybdate*: Causes serious eye irritation [H319].
                 *Classification/labelling vary. Suppliers may indicate: Causes skin irritation [H315], May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
  WARNING        WEL (mg m-3): 5 (LTEL), 10 (STEL); soluble molybdenum compounds (as Mo)
Ammonium ethanoate                     ammonium acetate                                                                 NH4CH3COO (77.08)
Ammonium sulfate(VI)                                                                                                     (NH4)2SO4 (132.14)
Currently not classified as hazardous.
                 Storage code: GIn                                                                   [Colourless solids]
                 • Ethanoate salt is hygroscopic (absorb water from the air).
                 • The reagent sold as ‘ammonium carbonate’ is usually a 1:1 mixture of ammonium carbamate
Storage
                   (NH2COONH4) and ammonium hydrogencarbonate (NH4HCO3). This mixture is designed to have the same
                   ammonium content as ammonium carbonate. Solid decomposes to ammonia and carbon dioxide.
                 • Keep container lids firmly closed.


Emergencies      Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

11 — Barium chromate(VI), nitrate(V) and peroxide

PDF pages 47–48
PDF page 47
11 Risk Assessment Guidance                             Barium chromate(VI), nitrate(V) and peroxide
Barium chromate(VI)                                                                                                BaCrO4 (253.32)
Barium nitrate(V)                                                                                               Ba(NO3)2 (261.34)
Barium peroxide                                                                                                      BaO2 (169.33)
                 May intensify fire; oxidiser [H272]. Harmful if swallowed [H302]. Harmful if inhaled [H332].
                 Barium nitrate(V) is dangerous in contact with:
                 • CARBON, SULFUR, POWDERED METALS. Readily ignites - is extremely sensitive to friction or impact.

                 Barium peroxide is dangerous in contact with:
                 • COMBUSTIBLE MATERIAL including ORGANIC SUBSTANCES. Violent or explosive reactions occur. May
                   ignite spontaneously, particularly if damp.
                 • POWDERED METALS. Dangerous reactions occur.
                 • ETHANOIC ACID and ETHANOIC ANHYDRIDE. Explosions occur.
                 • WATER. Vigorous reaction occurs forming a corrosive solution. Oxygen gas is rapidly evolved.
   DANGER
                 WEL (mg m-3):    0.5 (LTEL), 1.5 (STEL); as barium (Ba) in soluble compounds.
                                  0.01 (LTEL), 0.03 (STEL), Carc, Sen; as chromium (Cr) for barium chromate(VI).
                 Storage code: Situ (chromate)                                                                     [Yellow solid]
                 Storage code: Ox (nitrate; peroxide)                   [Colourless-white hygroscopic crystals; Grey-white solid]
Storage
                 • Keep barium peroxide dry. The solid decomposes in water to produce oxygen gas. Barium peroxide tins
                   often split after keeping for several years.

                 Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                 • Barium peroxide in the mouth/swallowed: Immediately call 999. This substance can cause serious
Emergencies
                   internal damage due to the release of oxygen gas.
                 • General spills/clearing up: OXIDISING. Keep dry while collecting up (barium peroxide).

solutions

                        Follow general guidance in About Hazcards (GL 120). NOTE for small amounts only:
                        • WSpec for barium nitrate(V): Dissolve the solid in water then add 1 M sodium carbonate to precipitate
                          barium carbonate. Filter off the solid (barium carbonate) for disposal in normal refuse, W8. Rinse the
Disposal                  aqueous filtrate (sodium nitrate) down a foul-water drain with plenty of water.
                        • WSpec for barium peroxide: Add no more than 5 g in small portions to 1 litre of 1 M sulfuric(VI) acid in a
                          beaker. Leave stirring overnight. Allow solid to settle then decant the liquid layer down a foul-water drain
                          with plenty of water. The solid barium sulfate(VI) can go in the normal refuse, W8.

Benzene-1,2-diol      catechol, pyrocatechol, 1,2-dihydroxybenzene (o-dihydroxybenzene)                       (HO)2C6H4 (110.11)
                      Toxic if swallowed and in contact with skin [H301, H311]. Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious

                      WEL (mg m-3): 23 (LTEL), 69 (STEL)

                      Both: Harmful if swallowed [H302]. May cause an allergic skin reaction [H317]. Very toxic to aquatic
                      organisms [H400].
                      Benzene-1,3-diol: Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. Causes damage to

                      Storage code: GOrg                                               [White or colourless crystalline solids]
Storage
                      • These compounds are best stored out of direct light.

These substances are dangerous in contact with:
• CONCENTRATED NITRIC(V) ACID. A vigorous (possibly explosive) reaction occurs.

                      Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies
                      • CORROSIVE (eyes): benzene-1,4-diol. TOXIC (ingestion, skin): benzene-1,2-diol.

15A — (see also 15B) Bromine liquid, Br2(l)

PDF pages 63–64
PDF page 63
15A Risk Assessment Guidance (see also 15B)                                                          Bromine liquid, Br2(l)
Bromine                                                                                                                  Br2 (160.0)
                   Fatal if inhaled [H330]. Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314]. Very toxic to aquatic organisms [H400].
                   Bromine liquid is dangerous in contact with:
                    AMMONIA solution (concentrated). An explosive product is formed.
                    SODIUM, POTASSIUM, ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM, MERCURY; ALCOHOLS, ETHERS and other organic
                     compounds. Violent or very violent reactions occur.
                   WEL (mg m-3): 0.66 (LTEL); 1.3 (STEL). See Emergencies (inhalation) below.
    DANGER
                   Storage code: Spec, see notes below                         [Dark red-brown volatile liquid; brown-orange fumes]
                    Keep the following next to liquid bromine at all times: At least 500 cm3 of 1 M sodium carbonate and also a
                      container of solid hydrated sodium carbonate (washing soda) for treating spills on hard surfaces.
                    Bromine liquid supplied in bottles: Place bottle inside another lidded container with soda lime to absorb fumes
Storage              (renew this regularly). This container can then be kept on shelves with general inorganics (GIn) in a secure
                     store. Regularly check condition of bottle caps/container lids; they can split. Purchase a spare cap so it can be
                     replaced immediately if there is any sign of a leak. Purchase only small quantities (100 cm3 or less).
                    Bromine liquid supplied in ampoules: Keep ampoules (usually 1 cm3 of bromine/ampoule) in their protective
                      packaging with other corrosives. Take only the required number of ampoules to prep room or laboratory.

                   Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                    VERY TOXIC (inhalation), BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS.
                    CORROSIVE (skin, eyes): Liquid and vapour.
                    General spills/clearing up. If more than 0.2 cm3: Immediately evacuate the spill area, open windows and
Emergencies          external doors (if safe to do so), switch on fans etc. Prevent access to the area. Consider if wider evacuation is
                     required. If safe to do so: re-enter after 1 hour and treat the spill area. Much depends on the volume involved
                     (eg, a bottle/ampoule breaking or spilling) but it may be necessary to call the Fire and Rescue Service.
                     If less than 0.2 cm3 (i.e. just a few drops): Add solid hydrated sodium carbonate (or 1 M sodium carbonate
                     solution) then clear up as usual.

15B — (see also 15A) Bromine water, Br2(aq)

PDF pages 65–66
PDF page 65
15B Risk Assessment Guidance (see also 15A)                                                      Bromine water, Br2(aq)
Bromine                                                                                                                        Br2 (160.0)
                   Fatal if inhaled [H330]. Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314]. Very toxic to aquatic organisms [H400].
                     The hazard information here relates to that of pure bromine (liquid and vapour). See Hazcard 15A.
                     Classification of aqueous bromine solutions (‘bromine water’) depends on concentration (see reverse).
                     Note also Emergencies information (see below).
                   Bromine (liquid) is dangerous in contact with:
                    AMMONIA solution (concentrated). An explosive product is formed.
                    SODIUM, POTASSIUM, ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM, MERCURY; ALCOHOLS, ETHERS and other organic
    DANGER           compounds. Violent or very violent reactions occur.
                   WEL (mg m-3): 0.66 (LTEL); 1.3 (STEL) as bromine. See also Emergencies (inhalation) below.
                   Storage code: GIn                                                                   [Orange-pale yellow solution]
                    Bromine vapour diffuses from solutions. Fumes affect the respiratory system and will accelerate the
                     corrosion of metals. Do not store in metal cabinets.
Storage             Bromine water becomes paler as bromine is lost (by diffusion), especially in warm conditions. Check that the
                     solution gives desired effect for the practical activity being undertaken.
                    Prepare aqueous bromine solutions just before use. Store in screw-top glass bottles (avoid using ‘polystop’
                     lids). Regularly check the condition of container lids; they will discolour and can split. Replace if necessary.

                   Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                    VERY TOXIC (inhalation), BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS: Bromine vapour.
                    General spills/clearing up: Much depends on the volume and concentration of solution.
Emergencies
                     If safe to do so: Ventilate the area as much as possible. Use disposable paper towels or other absorbent for
                     small spills. If affected by fumes, move out of the area to fresh air and take steps to prevent access to the area
                     of the spill. See also Hazcard 15A.

Read this Hazcard in conjunction with About Hazcards (Guide GL 120)                           Hazcards 2016 Edition ©CLEAPSS (Updated: 11/22)
PDF page 66
15B Risk Assessment Guidance (see also 15A)                                                                               Bromine water, Br2(aq)
BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS. Bromine is acutely toxic by inhalation. Effects of exposure by inhalation of bromine can increase over time.
Inhalation by those with known breathing difficulties (eg, asthma) may exacerbate such pre-existing conditions. If affected, call the
emergency services, informing them of the quantity/concentration of bromine involved.
Bromine vapour diffuses from solutions. At concentrations ≥ 0.01 M, the WEL (STEL) is rapidly approached in localised situations (eg, just
above open test-tubes or bottles) and inhalation of vapour would act at least as a respiratory irritant. Take this into account in addition to
the information below. It is advisable to include a warning to this effect on any labels used on prepared solutions (see suggested control
measures for additional guidance on what to include).
Detailed guidance on specific activities and techniques involving this substance can be found at: www.cleapss.org.uk

PDF page 67
16 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                            Calcium and strontium
Calcium                                                                                                                             Ca (40.08)
Strontium                                                                                                                           Sr (87.62)
                      Calcium: In contact with water releases flammable gases [H261].
                      Strontium: In contact with water releases flammable gases which may ignite spontaneously [H260]. Causes skin
                      irritation [H315].
          Strontium
                      These substances are dangerous in contact with:
                       WATER, ACIDS. Hydrogen gas is given off which may ignite from the heat of reaction (in some circumstances).
     DANGER            SULFUR. An explosive reaction occurs.
                       HYDROXIDES/CARBONATES of SODIUM, POTASSIUM and other ALKALI METALS. Reactions may be explosive.

                      Storage code: FW                                  [Silver-grey metallic granules or irregular-size/shape pieces]
                       Calcium: A grey-white oxide layer may form on granules/pieces. Purchase small quantities (eg, 25 g) and
                        store in an air-tight container to minimise oxidation.
                        Note: It may be more difficult to purchase calcium metal in the form of the small, almost spherical,
Storage                 granules (~ 1-2 mm diameter) many are familiar with. Instead, the metal may now be supplied as
                        irregularly-sized/shaped pieces (eg, with sizes ranging from 2-6 mm, or over, in the same sample).
                        Variable surface area will affect how quickly the calcium oxidises and also how it reacts with water and
                        other reagents. See Other notes (on reverse).
                       Strontium: Sometimes supplied stored under argon. Once opened, the metal can be stored dry in an air-
                        tight container or stored under medicinal paraffin (as for barium).

                      Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                       CORROSIVE (eyes), alkali.
Emergencies            If metals catch fire: They are difficult to ignite but burn vigorously once lit and are then difficult to extinguish.
                        Extinguish small fires by smothering with clean, dry sand (keep a container of sand specifically for this
                        purpose).

18 Risk Assessment Guidance Calcium oxide; calcium and strontium hydroxides
Calcium oxide                    quicklime                                                                   CaO (56.08)
Calcium hydroxide                slaked lime                                                             Ca(OH)2 (74.09)
Strontium hydroxide-8-water hydrated strontium hydroxide                                           Sr(OH)2.8H2O (265.76)
              Calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide: Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye damage [H318].
              Strontium hydroxide: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314].
              All: May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
              Calcium oxide is dangerous in contact with:
              • WATER. Vigorous reaction occurs that generates heat. Dust may be ejected and enter eyes. Under some
                conditions, the temperature rise is sufficient to ignite combustible material.
               WEL (mg m-3): 2 (LTEL), 6 (STEL); 1 (LTEL), 4 (STEL), as respirable dust; calcium oxide
  DANGER
                                 5 (LTEL), 15 (STEL); 1 (LTEL), 4 (STEL), as respirable dust; calcium hydroxide
               Storage code: CS                                                          [White crystalline solids or powders]
               • Solids react with atmospheric carbon dioxide and, once the container is opened, will deteriorate quite
                 rapidly. Older samples of the solids may not react as expected in practical activities.
               • Calcium oxide also reacts with moisture to form the hydroxide. Containers have been known to burst
Storage
                 due to expansion as the oxide becomes hydrated. Storing the container of calcium oxide inside another
                 (eg, plastic, lidded box or a strong plastic bag) will minimise powder spills if the original container bursts.
               • Purchase small quantities and only when required. Check state of containers and their contents on a
                 regular basis (eg, once per term). If any signs of deterioration, dispose of as W1.

            Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies • CORROSIVE (skin, eyes, inhalation), alkali: Solids and solutions.
            • General spills (solid): Large-scale spills (eg, a burst container) can be difficult to deal with. Contact CLEAPSS.

                 Anhydrous calcium chloride is dangerous in contact with:
  WARNING        • WATER. Anhydrous calcium chloride can cause water to boil.

                 Storage code: GIn                                                                     [Colourless/white solids]
 Storage
                 • These compounds absorb water from the atmosphere (i.e. are hygroscopic).


 Calcium fluoride                also fluorite, fluorspar (eg, Blue John)                                            CaF2 (78.075)
                 Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
                 Note: Classification/labelling vary and may differ from that given here.
                 Calcium fluoride is dangerous in contact with:
                 • CONCENTRATED ACIDS. Hydrogen fluoride is produced: corrosive, very toxic (inhalation, ingestion, skin).
  WARNING
                 WEL (mg m-3): 2.5 (LTEL), 7.5 (STEL) as fluoride
                 Storage code: GIn                                                         [Colourless/white crystalline solid]
 Storage         • Calcium fluoride is a colourless, almost insoluble compound. The naturally occurring mineral
                   (fluorite/fluorspar) is often deeply coloured due to impurities (eg, Blue John).

 Emergencies Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

19C — Calcium carbide & calcium phosphide

PDF pages 77–78
PDF page 77
19C Risk Assessment Guidance                                          Calcium carbide & calcium phosphide
Calcium carbide      calcium dicarbide, calcium acetylide                                                                CaC2 (64.10)
                     In contact with water releases flammable gases which may ignite spontaneously [H260].
                     Note: Classification/labelling vary. Some suppliers may also indicate one or more of: Causes skin irritation
                     [H315]. Causes serious eye damage [H318]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335]. The GHS05 pictogram
                     (corrosive) would then be shown.
     DANGER          Calcium carbide is dangerous in contact with:
                     • WATER. Ethyne (acetylene) gas is produced.

                     Storage code: FW                                                                           [Grey-black solid]
                     • Calcium carbide is usually supplied as granules (see Other notes on reverse). If the solid has become
Storage
                       white or has a white surface, then it is deteriorating. The white solid is calcium hydroxide.
                     • Regularly examine tins of calcium carbide for signs of rust.

Calcium phosphide                                                                                                 Ca3P2 (182.18)
                     In contact with water releases flammable gases which may ignite spontaneously [H260]. Contact with
                     water liberates toxic gas [EUH029]. Contact with acids liberates very toxic gas [EUH032]. Fatal if
                     swallowed [H300]. Toxic in contact with skin [H311]. Fatal if inhaled [H330]. Causes serious eye damage
                     [H318]. Very toxic to aquatic life [H400].
                     Calcium phosphide is dangerous in contact with:
                     • WATER, ACIDs. Phosphine gas (VERY TOXIC) forms; spontaneously ignites in air (due to diphosphine).
     DANGER          WEL (mg m-3): 0.14 (LTEL), 0.28 (STEL), phosphine.
Storage              Storage code: FW                                                                       [Red-brown/grey solid]
                     Follow standard procedures (See Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                     • If calcium carbide catches fire: Treat with a large excess of clean, dry sand.
Emergencies
                     • CORROSIVE (eyes): Calcium carbide, calcium phosphide.
                     • VERY TOXIC (ingestion, inhalation). TOXIC (skin): Calcium phosphide. Call 999.

phosphide                                                   • Demonstrations with calcium carbide: See Flammable ice.

                         *Calcium carbide: The resulting solution is alkaline (calcium hydroxide).

20B — Carbon disulfide, CS2

PDF pages 83–84
PDF page 83
20B Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                        Carbon disulfide, CS2
Carbon disulfide                                                                                                             CS2 (76.14)
                     Highly flammable liquid and vapour [H225]. Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye
                     irritation [H319]. Suspected of damaging fertility. Suspected of damaging the unborn child [H361fd].
                     Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure [H372].
                     Carbon disulfide is dangerous in contact with:
                      RUST. It may ignite the vapour.
                      ZINC and OTHER METAL POWDERS. Violent reactions occur.
                      PHOSPHORUS. The solution is highly dangerous.
                      NITROGEN OXIDE. An explosion may occur.

                        Not recommended for use in schools.
                        Any procedure involving carbon disulfide requires a Special Risk Assessment. Contact CLEAPSS.

     DANGER          WEL (mg m-3): 15 (LTEL), 45 (STEL), Sk           Flash point: − 30 oC

                     Storage code: FL                                                       [Colourless or pale yellow liquid]
Storage               The pure liquid has an ether-like smell but reagent grade samples have a foul ‘rotten-eggs’ odour due to
                       the presence of impurities.

Emergencies          Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

21 — Carbon monoxide, CO(g) and Carbon, C(s)

PDF pages 85–86
PDF page 85
21 Risk Assessment Guidance                                   Carbon monoxide, CO(g) and Carbon, C(s)
Carbon monoxide gas    carbonic oxide, coal gas                                                         CO (28.01)
                  Extremely flammable gas [H220]. Toxic if inhaled [H331]. May damage the unborn child [H360D].
                  Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure (inhalation) [H372].
                         Carbon monoxide gas has no taste or smell and can be very difficult to detect. It is produced
                         when carbon-based fuels burn without sufficient oxygen to ensure complete combustion.
                         Inhaled carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and impairs the ability of the blood to carry
                         and transfer oxygen. Even 0.01% (by volume) in air can cause headaches and dizziness.
                         Mixtures with air (between 12% and 74% carbon monoxide by volume) are explosive.
      DANGER             WEL (mg m-3): 23 (LTEL), 117 (STEL)

                       Storage code: Situ                                        [Colourless, odourless and tasteless gas]
Storage                • Gas cylinders are not recommended. Prepare small volumes of the gas in situ when required.
                         Be aware that the filters in recirculatory fume cupboards do NOT absorb this gas.
Carbon                 activated carbon, (activated/decolorising) charcoal, graphite, carbon black, lampblack   C (12.01)
Currently not          Carbon is dangerous in contact with:
classified as          • OXYGEN. Finely divided carbon is a fire hazard and carbon (or charcoal) blocks may catch fire if
hazardous but see        they are stacked or packed together whilst still hot.
other information      WEL (mg m-3): 3.5 (LTEL), 7 (STEL); carbon black
on this Hazcard.                        10 (LTEL), 30 (STEL); graphite (as inhalable dust)
Storage                Storage code: GIn, see also Other notes on reverse.

                       Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                       • General spills (carbon powders): Large-scale spills can be difficult to deal with without raising
Emergencies              airborne particles. Contact CLEAPSS for advice.
                       • Carbon monoxide: If a leak is suspected (eg, fume cupboard stops working), evacuate.

Chlorobenzene                 phenyl chloride                                                                                    C6H5Cl (112.56)
Bromobenzene                  phenyl bromide                                                                                     C6H5Br (157.01)
                              Both: Flammable liquid and vapour [H226]. Causes skin irritation [H315]. Toxic to aquatic life with long
                              lasting effects [H411]. Chlorobenzene: Harmful if inhaled [H332].

1,4-dichlorobenzene           p-dichlorobenzene                                                                                 C6H4Cl2 (147.00)
                              Both: Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. Very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects [H410].

28 — Dichloromethane

PDF pages 105–106
PDF page 105
28 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                             Dichloromethane
Dichloromethane methylene dichloride, methylene chloride, DCM                                                          CH2Cl2 (84.93)
                Suspected of causing cancer [H351]. Note: Hazard classification and labelling varies. Suppliers may indicate one
                or more of: Causes skin and serious eye irritation [H315, H319]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335]. May cause
                drowsiness or dizziness [H336]. May cause damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure [H373].
                Dichloromethane is dangerous in contact with:
                • AIR. HEAT. Flammable in air if heated above room temperature. Emits toxic fumes (hydrogen chloride,
                  carbon monoxide, phosgene) if heated to decomposition or if involved in combustion.
                • METHANOL. In the presence of methanol, the mixture is flammable at room temperature.
                • REACTIVE METALS (eg, ALKALI METALS, MAGNESIUM, ALUMINIUM). STRONG BASES. STRONG OXIDISING
                  AGENTS. Violent or explosive reactions can occur.
                • CONCENTRATED NITRIC(V) ACID. It may dissolve explosively and the solution can be detonated.
  WARNING
                WEL (mg m-3): 353 (LTEL), 706 (STEL), Sk

Storage         Storage code: GOrg                                                             [Colourless liquid, ‘sweet’ odour]

Dichloromethane is absorbed through the skin. It degreases the skin, which may lead to secondary inflammation. Exposure
through inhalation or ingestion may cause irritation to the respiratory tract, headaches, nausea, confusion, drowsiness and
dizziness. Eye contact with the vapour may cause irritation. More severe damage may occur through eye contact with the liquid.
Symptoms may or may not be immediately apparent and can develop and/or increase over time.
Avoid the use of dichloromethane in school practical activities (see reverse).

                Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                • CORROSIVE (eyes): liquid.
Emergencies     • BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS (eyes, inhalation, ingestion).
                • General spills: If more than a few cm3 are spilled outside a fume cupboard, leave the immediate area. Only
                  return when the spill has evaporated and dispersed.

30 — 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine

PDF pages 109–110
PDF page 109
30 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine          2,4-DNPH (used to prepare Brady’s reagent)                              (NO2)2C6H3NHNH2 (198.14)
                     Flammable solid [H228]. Harmful if swallowed [H302]. Some suppliers may also indicate one or more
                     of: Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319].
                     2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine is dangerous in contact with:
                     • OXIDISING AGENTS. METAL OXIDES. Vigorous or explosive reactions may occur.
                     • IGNITION SOURCE/SPARK. Risk of dust explosion if sufficient quantity of dry powder is in the air.

                         The storage and use of 2,4-DNPH is affected by the current Explosives Regulations.
     DANGER              See Fireworks and explosives. Contact CLEAPSS for further advice.
                     Storage code: T (Organic)                                                                [Orange-red solid]
                     • The solid is supplied ‘wetted’ to minimise the risk of explosion. To keep the solid damp, stand the
                       bottle inside a larger (labelled) container that also contains a little tap water (~ 1 cm depth).
Storage
                       Protect the bottle’s label.
                     • If incorrectly stored, the solid may have become dry and more sensitive to shock or friction.
                       Do NOT attempt to open the bottle; contact CLEAPSS.
Phenylhydrazine                                                                                                           C6H8N2 (108.14)
                                                               Do NOT use this compound.
                     Toxic if swallowed, in contact with skin & if inhaled [H301, H311, H331]. Causes skin and serious eye irritation [H315,
                     H319]. May cause an allergic skin reaction [H317]. Suspected of causing genetic defects [H341]. May cause cancer
          DANGER     [H350]. Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure [H372]. Very toxic to aquatic life [H400].

                     Storage code: T (Organic)                            [Colourless-yellow liquid/solid (melting point is ~ 20 oC)]
Storage
                     • Storage is prior to disposal, W1.

                     Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies
                     • General spills, 2,4-DNPH: Keep moist. Scoop into a suitable container. Thoroughly rinse spill area.

33 — Enzymes

PDF pages 115–116
PDF page 115
33 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                                    Enzymes
Enzymes
Enzymes are proteins found in living organisms. They can be extracted & purchased in various forms (eg, powders, solutions).
Hazard classifications for enzymes and enzyme preparations vary but the majority are sensitisers. Many are skin, eye and
respiratory irritants and some may cause serious eye damage.
Commercial suppliers may indicate one or more of the following for their enzyme product(s). Some may indicate no hazard
classification. Check supplier’s information.

                              DANGER                                  DANGER                                   WARNING

          May cause allergy or asthma symptoms          Causes serious eye damage [H318]   Causes skin irritation [H315]
          or breathing difficulties if inhaled [H334]                                      Causes serious eye irritation [H319]
                                                                                           May cause respiratory irritation [H335]

                  Storage code: Cold (see notes below)                             [Supplied in different forms: powders, liquids etc]
                   Storage conditions: Check supplier’s information and/or other detailed CLEAPSS guidance.
                   Enzymes from natural sources: Prepare as required. It is important to check activity-specific guidance.
Storage
                   Commercial sources of enzymes: Properties may differ markedly depending on the source organism.
                    Check before purchase that the enzyme is suitable for the intended use.
                   Discard enzymes when out of date or no longer active.


            Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies  General spills: Large-scale spills (eg, a burst container of a fine powder) can be difficult to deal with. Do
              not put yourself in danger of exposure to enzymes by skin/eye contact or by inhalation. If unsure how
              to proceed, contact CLEAPSS.

34 — Ethanal and its tetramer

PDF page 117
34 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                               Ethanal and its tetramer
Ethanal               acetaldehyde                                                                                 CH3CHO (44.05)
                      Extremely flammable liquid and vapour [H224]. Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. May cause
                      respiratory irritation [H335]. Suspected of causing genetic effects [H341]. May cause cancer [H350].
                      Ethanal is dangerous in contact with:
                      • SULFURIC(VI) ACID AND OTHER ACIDS. Violent polymerisation reactions may occur.
                      • SILVER NITRATE SOLUTION. Explosive products are formed.

            DANGER     Note:              Flash point (oC)   Boiling point (oC)         WEL (mg m−3)
                                                −39                  21              37 (LTEL); 92 (STEL)
                      Storage code: FL (Organic)                                  [Colourless liquid, pungent, irritating odour]
                      • Ethanal’s boiling point is low (‘room temperature’). It has been known to spontaneously boil away
Storage
                        during storage and on opening. Open bottles in a fume cupboard - see Other notes (on reverse).
                      • Ethanal gradually oxidises to ethanoic acid during storage.


Metaldehyde           ethanal tetramer, 2,4,6,8-tetramethyl-1,3,5,7-tetraoxacyclooctane                        (CH3CHO)4 (176.22)



                      Flammable solid [H228]. Toxic if swallowed [H301]. Suspected of damaging fertility [H361f].
                      Harmful to aquatic life with long lasting effects [H412].
            DANGER

                      Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:

                      • General spills (ethanal): EXTREMELY FLAMMABLE, VOLATILE.

2-hydroxypropanoic acid       lactic acid                                                                    CH3CH(OH)COOH (90.08)
                             Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes serious eye damage [H318].
                DANGER       Note: Some suppliers may indicate Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314] and Corrosive to the
                             respiratory tract [EUH071]; these appear to relate specifically to the L-(+)- isomer.

                             Storage code: CLa or CS (Organic)*                                     [Colourless-yellow liquid/solid*]
Storage
                             *Lactic acid exists in different isomeric forms. Physical state and properties vary.

Amino acids                                                                                                                       (various)
Ascorbic acid                Vitamin C                                                                                   C6H8O6 (176.12)
Gibberellic acid                                                                                                       C19H22O6 (346.37)
Hormone rooting powders                                                                                                           (various)
Indol-3-ylethanoic acid      indolylacetic acid, indoleacetic acid, IAA                                               C10H9NO2 (175.18)
Indol-3-ylbutanoic acid      indolylbutyric acid, indolebutyric acid, IBA                                            C12H13NO2 (203.24)
Currently not classified as hazardous.
Note: Classification and labelling vary. Some suppliers may indicate one or more of: Causes skin irritation [H315]. Causes
serious eye irritation [H319]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].

Storage                      Storage code: GOrg                                                               [Colourless/white solids]

Emergencies                  Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

39 — Ethanoic anhydride

PDF pages 141–142
PDF page 141
39 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                       Ethanoic anhydride
Ethanoic anhydride           acetic anhydride                                                              (CH3CO)2O (102.09)
                      Flammable liquid and vapour [H226]. Harmful if swallowed or if inhaled [H302, H332]. Causes severe
                      skin burns and eye damage [H314]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
                      Note: Suppliers may indicate - Toxic if inhaled [H331] and include the GHS06 pictogram.
                      Ethanoic anhydride is dangerous in contact with:
                      • WATER. The hydrolysis reaction is very vigorous. In the presence of ethanoic acid (which is formed
                        anyway), the reaction can become violent.
                      • ETHANOL. If acid is present, the reaction is vigorous.
                      • BORIC ACID, CHROMIUM(VI) OXIDE, MANGANATES(VII), NITRIC(V) ACID, PEROXIDES. Violent or
     DANGER             explosive reactions may occur.
                      WEL (mg m-3): 2.5 (LTEL), 10 (STEL)             Flash point: 49 oC
                      Storage code: CW (Organic)                                        [Colourless liquid, pungent odour]
Storage               • Purchase small quantities. Regularly check the condition of bottle tops/caps, replace if required.
                      • Place the bottle inside another container that also contains soda lime (to absorb any fumes).

                      Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                      • CORROSIVE (eyes, skin).

                      • CORROSIVE/TOXIC (inhalation). BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS.

                      • General spills: FLAMMABLE, CORROSIVE-WATER REACTIVE. Odours are pungent & unpleasant.
Emergencies
                        If safe to deal with: Ventilate the area as much as possible. Cover spill with absorbent. Scoop into a
                        dry bucket and take to a fume cupboard. Treat with a large excess of water (eg, use 4 L for a 100 cm3
                        spill). Leave to hydrolyse for at least 12 hours. [Thoroughly mop spill area.] After 12 hours, decant the
                        liquid (now a solution of ethanoic acid) down a foul-water drain and rinse away with more water.
                        Place rinsed absorbent in the waste.

40A — Ethanol (and IDA)

PDF pages 143–144
PDF page 143
40A Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                   Ethanol (and IDA)
Pure ethanol is expensive, and schools and colleges usually buy industrial denatured alcohol (IDA) but label it ‘ethanol’. Denatured
alcohol is alcohol that has been treated to make it unsuitable for drinking. IDA (once called industrial methylated spirits, IMS) contains
ethanol plus 5% of, usually, wood naphtha (mainly methanol), which results in the additional health hazard classification.
Completely denatured alcohol (CDA) is a mixture of ethanol, propan-2-ol and methyl ethyl ketone. A bitter-tasting compound is added
and, sometimes, a blue/purple dye. CDA, also known as mineralised methylated spirits, is not suitable for school science activities.
Ethanol                Ethyl alcohol                                                                                      CH3CH2OH (46.07)
                       Pure ethanol: Highly flammable liquid and vapour [H225].
                       IDA is also: Harmful if swallowed [H302]. May cause damage to organs [H371]. (GHS 07 & GHS 08 pictograms).
                       Some suppliers may also include: Causes serious eye irritation [H319] for ethanol or IDA.
                       This substance (ethanol or IDA) is dangerous in contact with:
                       • BROMINE. Violent reaction may occur.
                       • MERCURY(II) and SILVER NITRATE(V). Explosive fulminates may be formed.
                       • OXIDISING AGENTS. Uncontrollable reactions take place, especially with NITRIC(V) ACID.
                       • PLATINUM. Finely divided metal (eg, platinised electrodes, catalysts) may cause ethanol to burst into flame.
                       • POTASSIUM. An explosive reaction will occur.
     DANGER            WEL (mg m-3): 1920 (LTEL), 5760 (STEL); ethanol               Flash point: 13 oC
                                         266 (LTEL), 333 (STEL), Sk; methanol
                       Storage code: FL (Organic)                                                                         [Colourless liquid]
                       • Keep main stock containers under lock and key. Records need to be kept of the volume of IDA ordered and used
                         by the school (normally covered by good stocktaking procedures).
Storage
                       • To purchase and use more than 5 litres per year of IDA, the school will need to provide a supplier with a copy of
                         the Excise Notice 473 authorisation it has obtained from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). See Ethanol – HM
                         Revenue & Customs (HMRC) – Application Form in the Useful Links section of the CLEAPSS science website.

                       Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies            • If swallowed: Monitor for signs of intoxication. If more than a few cm3 have been swallowed or if concerned,
                         call the emergency services and tell them the quantity of chemical(s) involved.

42 — Ethoxyethane and other ethers

PDF pages 151–152
PDF page 151
42 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                    Ethoxyethane and other ethers
Ethoxyethane           diethyl ether, ether                                                         C2H5OC2H5 (74.12)
                Extremely flammable liquid and vapour [H224]. Harmful if swallowed [H302]. May cause drowsiness or
                dizziness [H336]. May form explosive peroxides [EUH019]. Repeated exposure may cause skin dryness or
                cracking [EUH066].
                Ethoxyethane is dangerous in contact with:
                 OXIDISING AGENTS. Risk of explosive reactions.
                 BROMINE AND CHLORINE. Explosive reactions occur. Ignition occurs on contact with chlorine.

                 WEL (mg m-3): 310 (LTEL), 620 (STEL)        Flashpoint: − 45 oC
                 Do not have naked flames in the same room as ethoxyethane. This liquid has a low boiling point (~ 34 oC) and
   DANGER        the vapour (more dense than air) may rapidly spread over a wide area and/or collect in pockets. ‘Flashback’
                 from any ignition source may occur. Ethoxyethane contains tiny amounts of peroxide (explosive), which will
                 increase when exposed to air after bottle is opened; it is normally sold with inhibitors to reduce this risk.

Methoxybenzene         anisole, methyl phenyl ether                                                            CH3OC6H5 (108.14)
                Flammable liquid and vapour [H226]. May cause drowsiness or dizziness [H336]. Causes skin irritation [H315].
                Causes serious eye irritation [H319]. Repeated exposure may cause skin dryness or cracking [EUH066].
                Flashpoint: 52 oC
  WARNING

                Storage code: FL (Organic)                                            [Colourless liquids with ‘sweet’ odours]
                 Ethoxyethane: Do not put anything treated with ether into a refrigerator that is not specially spark-
Storage           proofed; the door switch may ignite the vapour. Dispose of any ethoxyethane older than 2 years.
                 Methoxybenzene: The ‘aniseed-like’ odour can linger. If there is not enough room in the flammables
                  cabinet, this chemical can be stored with GOrg.

Emergencies Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

47A — Hydrochloric acid

PDF pages 173–174
PDF page 173
47A Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                           Hydrochloric acid
Hydrochloric acid                                                                                         HCl(aq) (36.46)
              Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314]. May cause respiratory irritation [H335].
              Note: Some suppliers also indicate: May be corrosive to metals [H290]. The GHS 05 pictogram (and WARNING)
              may then be indicated on solutions below 6.8 M (see reverse).
                Hydrochloric acid (concentrated) is dangerous in contact with:
                • REACTIVE METALS (e.g. SODIUM, MAGNESIUM, CALCIUM, ALUMINIUM). Violent reactions can occur.
                • POTASSIUM MANGANATE(VII). Explosions can occur.
                • SULFURIC(VI) and PHOSPHORIC(V) ACIDs (concentrated). Hydrogen chloride gas may be released.

   DANGER       WEL (mg m-3): 2 (LTEL), 8 (STEL); hydrogen chloride gas and aerosol mist.
                                 Hydrogen chloride gas (toxic, corrosive) diffuses from concentrated acid solutions.
                Storage code: CLa                                                            [Colourless to pale-yellowish liquid]
                • Usually purchased as a 35-38% (w/w) solution.
                • Once bottles are opened, hydrogen chloride gas can leak out into the store and accelerate metal corrosion.
                  Firmly close bottles after use. Older bottles of acid may not be the expected concentration.
Storage         • Hydrogen chloride gas can also diffuse through plastic; labels on containers will fade and eventually
                  disintegrate. Containers themselves may become damaged and/or the acid darkens over time. Check the
                  state of containers, lids and labels on a regular basis. If required, decant solutions into fresh containers.
                • Hydrogen chloride gas reacts with ammonia and amines. A white powder (chloride salts) will deposit on
                  bottles and elsewhere in the chemical store indicating (i) leaking bottles or lids (ii) acid or ammonia/amine
                  vapours diffusing through plastic bottles (iii) inadequate ventilation in the store.

            Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
            • CORROSIVE (skin, eyes).
Emergencies
            • CORROSIVE, TOXIC (inhalation). Procedures or reactions may liberate hydrogen chloride gas and/or
              produce chlorine gas. See also Hazcards 49 and 22A.

48 — Hydrogen, H2(g)

PDF pages 179–180
PDF page 179
48 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                   Hydrogen, H2(g)
Hydrogen                                                                                                                 H2 (2.02)
              Extremely flammable gas [H220]. If cylinder/canister: Contains gas under pressure; may explode if heated [H280].
              Hydrogen gas is dangerous in contact with:
              • OXYGEN, CHLORINE. Explosive reactions occur.
              • TRANSITION METALS and TRANSITION METAL OXIDES. These substances, under certain circumstances, lower the
                activation energy and ignition temperature of the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen.
               • Hydrogen/air mixtures are explosive over the range of 4% - 75% by volume of hydrogen. The ignition
                  temperature of these mixtures is 500 oC, which is lower than the temperature of a Bunsen burner flame.
                  Ignition can occur well below this temperature in the presence of transition metals or their oxides.
  DANGER       • Never oil or grease gas cylinder valves or fittings.
               • Never attempt to breathe hydrogen to change the pitch of the voice.

              Storage code: Cyl or Situ                                            [Colourless, odourless gas. Less dense than air.]
              • Cyl: Refillable cylinders may be hired. Non-refillable canisters are available to purchase. Depending on
                requirements, non-refillable canisters offer advantages (storage, manual handling, small quantities) and may be a
                viable alternative. See Gas cylinders for detailed guidance on pressurised gas containers.
                • Ensure the location of all pressurised gas cylinders/canisters is recorded and known to the site manager.

                • Cylinder (refillable): When fitted with a regulator, the cylinder is considered as ‘being held ready for use’ (rather

                  than ‘stored’). Keep cylinder upright (chained or clamped) and in a cool, well-ventilated area but not in the same
Storage           place where flammables or radioactives are stored. Carry out a visual check of the apparatus whenever it is used.
                  Check and follow up-to-date guidance on maintenance.
                  A two-stage regulator (i.e. a needle valve + pressure-reducing valve) is recommended as it provides the fine
                  control of gas flow and gas pressure necessary for some practical procedures that use hydrogen gas.
                • Canister (non-refillable): Store on its side (with mini flow valve/regulator removed) in a suitable container (so it

                  does not roll), on the shelves of a secure chemical store. Do not place the canister in the flammables cupboard.
              • Situ: Chemically-generated hydrogen gas is not appropriate for some situations. See Other notes on reverse.

Emergencies Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120).

51A — Hydrogen sulfide gas and solution

PDF pages 185–186
PDF page 185
51A Risk Assessment Guidance                                             Hydrogen sulfide gas and solution
Hydrogen sulfide                                                                                                       H2S (34.08)
                       Extremely flammable gas [H220]. Fatal if inhaled [H330]. Very toxic to aquatic organisms [H400].
                       Hydrogen sulfide gas is dangerous in contact with:
                       • MANY REAGENTS including: PEROXIDES, many OXIDISING AGENTS and some METAL OXIDES. These
                         can cause the gas to ignite.
                       • AIR. Explosive mixtures may form.
                       • SODA LIME. The gas is absorbed exothermically. If air is present the soda lime may become red hot.

                       WEL (mg m-3): 7 (LTEL), 14 (STEL)
                         Hydrogen sulfide gas is extremely toxic. It affects the nervous, cardiovascular and respiratory
      DANGER             systems as well as causing eye/skin irritation.
                         The pungent smell is usually sufficient to ensure that rapid evasive action is taken but be aware
                         that above a certain concentration the ability to detect hydrogen sulfide by smell is lost.

                       Storage code: Situ                               [Colourless gas, denser than air; rotten eggs odour]
                       • Prepare small volumes of hydrogen sulfide gas only when required. Do not use cylinders as school
Storage
                         fume cupboards will not cope with a rapid and large volume release of this gas under pressure.
                       • Check that the fume cupboard is working efficiently before preparing and using this gas.


                       Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies            • GAS RELEASE: If a leak occurs/is suspected (eg, fume cupboard stops working), evacuate.

                       • If inhaled: Immediately call 999.

51B — Hydrogen sulfide: soluble salts

PDF page 187
51B Risk Assessment Guidance                                                     Hydrogen sulfide: soluble salts
Sulfide salts absorb moisture and gases from the atmosphere and produce hydrogen sulfide gas. Hydrogen sulfide gas is
extremely toxic. It affects the nervous, cardiovascular and respiratory systems and causes eye/skin irritation. See Hazcard 51A.

Ammonium sulfide (available as ~ 20 % (w/v) solution)                                                               (NH4)2S (68.14)

                           Flammable liquid and vapour [H226]*. Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314].
                           Contact with acids liberates toxic gas [EUH031]. Very toxic to aquatic organisms [H400].
                           * May not be indicated; flash point depends on composition. Check supplier’s information.
          DANGER
                           Storage code: CLb                                                     [Colourless-yellow liquid]
Storage                    • At room temperature ammonium sulfide is only stable in aqueous solution. The solution is
                             actually a mixture containing ammonium hydrogen sulfide and ammonia.

Potassium sulfide                                                                                              K2S (110.26)
Sodium sulfide-9-water                                                                                 Na2S.9H2O (240.22)
                           Harmful if swallowed [H302]. Toxic in contact with skin [H311]. Causes severe skin burns and
                           eye damage [H314]. Contact with acids liberates toxic gas [EUH031]. Very toxic to aquatic
                           organisms [H400].
          DANGER                                  Potassium sulfide is NOT suitable for use in schools.

                           Storage code: CS                                                      [Colourless-yellow solid]
Storage                    • Solid absorbs moisture and gases from the atmosphere and produces hydrogen sulfide gas.
                             Store bottle inside another container with anhydrous calcium chloride (not soda lime).

                           Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
Emergencies                • CORROSIVE (skin, eyes): Solid, solutions. Solutions are strongly alkaline.
                           • If hydrogen sulfide gas is inhaled, call 999. See also Hazcard 51A.

54 — Iodine (solid and solutions), I2

PDF pages 193–194
PDF page 193
54 Risk Assessment Guidance                                                        Iodine (solid and solutions), I2
Iodine                                                                                                                     I2 (253.80)
                    Harmful in contact with skin [H312]. Harmful if inhaled [H332]. Very toxic to aquatic life [H400].
                    Iodine is dangerous in contact with:
                    • SODIUM, POTASSIUM, ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM, ZINC. Violent reactions occur. [Iodine solid]
                    • AMMONIA solution. An explosive solid is formed. [Iodine solid and solutions]
    WARNING
                    WEL (mg m-3): 1.1 (STEL) as iodine
                    Storage code: CS (solid); GIn (solutions)                                [Metallic grey solid, violet vapour]
                    • Solutions of iodine in other solvents (eg, ethanol) will have additional hazards. Consult Hazcards.
                    • The concentration of solutions decreases with storage; dilute solutions are particularly affected. Store in

Storage               screw-top glass bottles (avoid ‘polystop’ bottles). Plastic bottles (and caps) become discoloured.
                    • Vapour from iodine solid or solutions can escape out of poorly-sealed bottles; it accelerates the corrosion
                      of metals in the room and discolours labels. Place the bottle of solid iodine inside another lidded
                      container (which also contains a layer of soda lime). Regularly check condition of containers and for signs
                      of leakage. Replace if necessary.

                    Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                    • If spilt on skin/clothes: Quickly brush off as much dry solid as possible. Irrigate with plenty of water.
                      Note: solid/concentrated solutions can have a corrosive action on skin causing burns if left untreated.
                    • BEWARE DELAYED EFFECTS (eyes). If vapour affects the eyes, discomfort may be delayed for some hours.
Emergencies
                    • General spills/clearing up: Ventilate the area as much as possible.
                      • Solids: Scoop into 1 M sodium thiosulfate solution. Spread 0.5-1 M sodium thiosulfate solution over the

                         area of the spill. Leave for an hour. Mop up and rinse area. See Disposal.
                      • Solutions: Add absorbent. Wash area of spill with 0.5-1 M sodium thiosulfate solution if needed.

                Harmful if swallowed [H302]. Harmful if inhaled [H332]. May damage the unborn child. Suspected of damaging
                fertility [H360Df]. May cause harm to breast-fed children [H362] – lead metal. May cause damage to organs through
                prolonged or repeated exposure [H373]. Very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects [H410] – lead metal with
                particle size < 1 mm, and lead compounds.
                Lead oxides are dangerous in contact with:
                • ALUMINIUM, MAGNESIUM powders & ORGANIC material. Vigorous or explosive reactions may occur.

                 In schools these substances are used infrequently and in small quantities. Exposure through
                 ingestion or inhalation is, therefore, low and controlled, if the risk assessment advice is followed.
                 Lead and its compounds may be of concern to those who are pregnant (see Pregnant, new and
                 breastfeeding mothers and school science).
  DANGER
                Storage code: T
                • Lead metal: soft, dense silvery-grey metal (lead metal powder may appear very dark).
Storage
                • Lead(II) carbonates: colourless-white solids. Lead(II) sulfide: black solid (galena ore is silvery).
                • Lead oxides: red/red-brown solids (lead(II) oxide can exist in two forms, one is yellow).

                Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                • General spills: Avoid raising dust. Scoop and/or wipe up as much solid as possible. Retain all solid waste
Emergencies
                  and contaminated cloths/paper towels for disposal via a Registered Waste Carrier. Rinse the area with
                  water and clear up. The diluted washings may be flushed away down a foul-water drain.

58A — Lithium

PDF pages 207–208
PDF page 207
58A Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                                 Lithium
Lithium                                                                                                               Li (6.9)
                    In contact with water releases flammable gases which may ignite spontaneously [H260]. Reacts violently
                    with water [EUH014]. Causes severe skin burns and eye damage [H314].
                    Lithium is dangerous in contact with:
                    • NITRIC(V) ACID. The metal ignites on contact.

     DANGER         • 1, 1, 1-TRICHLOROETHANE and similar compounds. The metal reacts explosively.
                    • MERCURY. A violent reaction can occur.

                    Storage code: FW                                          [Silvery-white (when freshly cut) semi-soft metal]
                    • Store under paraffin liquid (‘medicinal paraffin’, see Hazcard 45B). Lithium will float, so some bottles
                      have a lid device to keep the metal pieces submerged (see Technician Tip: Storing lithium). Some lithium
                      pieces may look black if their surfaces have oxidised/tarnished. A ‘whiff’ of ammonia may briefly be
Storage               noticed when the lid is first removed (often if metal has not been kept submerged).
                    • Store away from water/water-based reagents. Do not store in the flammables cupboard or with
                      flammable liquids. Stand the bottle of lithium inside another clean, dry container (labelled) to keep it
                      upright. See Storage of chemicals.
                    • Purchase small quantities only (eg, 25 g will be adequate) so that stock is fresh.

                    Follow standard procedures (see Emergency Hazcards and GL 120). NOTE:
                    • CORROSIVE (skin, eyes), alkali.
                    • If lithium catches fire: Lithium burns vigorously and is difficult to extinguish. Smother small fires with clean,
                      dry sand (keep a container of this specifically for this purpose; see Technician Tip: Fire bucket alternative).
Emergencies         • General spills/clearing up: FLAMMABLE WATER-REACTIVE. Prevent spill from spreading. Use forceps to
                      pick up metal pieces. Place pieces in a clean, dry container, cover with fresh liquid paraffin and store for
                      disposal by a Registered Waste Carrier. Cover remaining spill with absorbent and scoop into a bucket of
                      cold water. Once any reaction is complete (may take time), dilute further. Pour down a foul-water drain.
                      Mop spill area but beware of possible reactions between the water and any remaining lithium fragments.


Read this Hazcard in conjunction with About Hazcards (Guide GL 120)                          Hazcards 2016 Edition ©CLEAPSS (Updated: 11/21)
PDF page 208
58A Risk Assessment Guidance                                                                                                                       Lithium
Take steps to prevent theft. After any use of lithium (eg, a demonstration), ensure that the bottle is securely locked away. In
addition, to ensure that a technician will not be faced with an unexpected reaction when clearing up, place any tiles plus the
equipment used to cut or handle pieces of lithium into a large bowl of cold water.
Detailed guidance on specific activities and techniques involving these substances can be found at: www.cleapss.org.uk

                                                                  place a piece of lithium onto a tile. Use a sharp knife to cut off required
                                                        TT        piece. Immediately return the unwanted lithium to its bottle and close lid.
Lithium                                                           Dab the cut piece of lithium with a paper tissue/filter paper to remove the
                                                       (Y9)
                               DANGER                             oil (medicinal paraffin). Do not use organic solvents (eg, petroleum spirit
                             (See reverse)                        or hexane) to remove the oil.

                                                                  Use safety screens. Lithium has been known to explode when heated on
                                                                  porcelain, so heat on the ceramic centre of a gauze, or on a combustion
                                                                  spoon.

                       Follow general guidance in About Hazcards (GL 120). NOTE for small amounts only:
Disposal               • W5: Add only a few small pieces of lithium at a time to 1 M ethanoic acid and allow reaction to subside
                         before adding further pieces. The reaction is not usually violent.
